blogs.title: When Expert Testimony Breaks Down: How Finesse v. AT&T Reinforces the Substantial‑Evidence Standard for JMOL
blogs.description: A deep dive into the Federal Circuit’s analysis of Dr. Jonathan Wells’s conflicting testimony about “signals of interest” and “interference‑generating signals.” The post explains why the court found the jury’s finding unsupported by substantial evidence, explores the interaction between Rule 702/Daubert considerations and the JMOL review standard, and offers practical guidance for patent litigators on structuring expert reports that can survive a de novo JMOL challenge.

blogs.title: Interpreting Functional Language in Telecom Patents: Claim Construction Lessons from ‘Signals’ and ‘Three Separately Identifiable Signals’
blogs.description: An examination of the court’s construction of key functional terms in the ’134 and ’775 patents—“signals of interest,” “interference generating signals,” and “three separately identifiable signals.” The article contrasts intrinsic versus extrinsic evidence, dissects the role of prosecution‑history estoppel in rejecting a “unique signal” requirement, and assesses how this decision may shape future claim‑construction disputes in wireless‑technology patents.

blogs.title: Amendments ≠ Surrender? Why Finesse Wireless’s Claim Amendments Did Not Limit Its Patent Scope
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Federal Circuit’s refusal to treat Finesse’s amendment from “two or three signals” to “three signals” as a clear disavowal of claim scope. It explains the legal thresholds for establishing claim surrender, cites relevant precedent (e.g., Continual Circuits v. Intel), and discusses the broader implications for patent owners who amend claims during prosecution—especially in high‑tech fields where functional limitations are common.
